She hadn’t even seen her come into the room until the glass had been picked up and carried away. And then she felt that she had seen the woman, though all she really remembered was the black-and-white uniform and the Fulcrum logo.

Someone else entered from the hallway and shut the door behind them.
“Is this everyone?” a deep male voice asked.

“Hey,” the new person said to Mara. He turned her way with his hand still on the doorknob. He wore dark glasses over one eye, as well as an expression that couldn’t decide whether to be amused or resigned. “Mara. Nice to meet you. Sorry I’m late. That was the wrong door; I’ve only ever come in through the back door, didn’t realize they had another one on this wing.”

She met his eyes and introduced herself.
He was younger than she expected; or if not young in years, he seemed younger than Jonah and the brown-haired man. “Adrian,” he said, “from the lab. I’m sorry we haven’t talked before now, I got busy and then I ended up here on short notice…”
“I thought that was just me.” Mara said it lightly, and with a smile; though she felt both glad and surprised to hear someone else saying, at Fulcrum, that he might have done better.
text:
When Mara walked into the common room at six fifteen, someone was already there. Someone younger, it seemed.
She couldn’t make out the face behind the blond hair. But the body was fine enough, leaning back on the couch with bare legs crossed and arms flung in opposite directions, one palm pressing the padded wall and the other wrist resting on the low table beside him.
She stood stock-still by the doorway for a moment, aware of her breath and of his awareness that she was here. He stirred and tilted his head; a face turned toward her, expressionless.

The two pairs of eyes held each other through an entire exhale.
And then the young man had pushed himself up on the armrests, stretched to his full height, and strolled over to shake her hand.
“Mara?”
He was closer than she would have guessed from where he’d been sitting, broad-shouldered and strong-chinned in a white T-shirt, grinning at her through dark-framed glasses as he reached out for the handshake. She took it.
“Jonah,” he said.
“Hello,” she replied, and then they stood there, still shaking hands, not knowing what to do next.

And that was when a door opened down the hallway behind her, releasing two voices into the room. One female, one male; one asking a question, the other replying; neither loud nor excited, just casual conversation. Jonah released her hand and turned away to look down the hall at them.
When Mara heard the voices and followed his gaze, she saw one young man who wasn’t Jonah, but close in size and shape; he had brown hair and a beard and was carrying a glass.

The brown-haired man glanced once over his shoulder, saw them standing there, nodded hello, and stepped right into the gathering, holding up his glass of wine—a half-full plastic cup with the Fulcrum logo on it. “Cheers.” He set it on the table against the wall to the left of the door, and stepped forward to shake Jonah’s hand as they exchanged names.

As he set down the glass and moved out of its space, a previously unseen catering worker entered from the hallway behind him and retrieved it. She wore the same black-and-white striped Fulcrum uniform shirt, though she looked old enough to have had that job since the Institute was founded; and she gave no outward sign of the social fact that she was taking their discarded drink back to the kitchen, while the rest of the conversation went on.

Mara watched this woman return to the hallway where she belonged, and noticed herself noticing who assumed whose labor.

That was just as odd, but at least it made sense in the world: somebody else had taken away the glass. A whole class of somebody else. She hadn’t even seen her come into the room until the glass had been picked up and carried away. And then she felt that she had seen the woman, though all she really remembered was the black-and-white uniform and the Fulcrum logo.

Someone else entered from the hallway and shut the door behind them.
“Is this everyone?” a deep male voice asked.

segment:
The next time the door opened, Mara looked over just in time to watch a pair of legs cross the threshold and disappear past her left elbow. Then she heard footsteps on the linoleum, followed by the creaking of an armchair and the click of a leather sole on tile, as its occupant moved away from the table by the hall door toward the couch that Jonah Reed had just vacated.
She turned her head to look.
It was Adrian, again—wearing the same suit as he’d been in before, only now with the jacket discarded on the floor behind him; the back of his white dress shirt, with its hidden buttons, was a little crumpled, but that might be where he’d just sat.

New manuscript after the continuation
He looked up when he caught her glance, smiled, and held out a hand, palm up.
She met his gaze for a moment longer, and then stepped toward him to take it. She couldn’t remember whether they’d shaken hands or not; she might have been holding that glass of water the whole time. He looked her in the eye as he shook, and said something, but her brain caught no words through the ringing.
“Did you say something?” Mara asked after the handshake ended, feeling both foolish and uncertain.

He looked at her for a long moment, and then smiled and took the chair that she’d been standing near—the one with his jacket still under it. It had been a question: “How are you feeling now?”
She opened her mouth to respond but then heard his voice again before the words came.
